cards.title: Your Next AI Project: Ditch the Cloud, Build a Personal, Always-On 'Brain' for Local Agents
cards.thesis: While everyone's buzzing about massive cloud AI models, there's a clear shift towards personal, local AI tools that give users more control and privacy. People are noticing that big cloud LLMs (like Claude) can be unreliable, leading to a demand for 'always-on' solutions that run on your own computer. This opens up a huge opportunity for builders to create the essential 'memory' layer for these personal AI assistants.

evidence.text: The 'Screen memory without screenshots' app is a macOS menu bar app that reads text from your focused window via the Accessibility API (a way for apps to interact with what's on your screen). It converts this into plain markdown files daily, allowing other AI tools (like Claude Code) to 'remember' your work and answer questions like 'what did I work on Tuesday?'.

People are asking 'Claude Is Down?' and wondering 'When Claude is down, do they have a backup Claude to investigate the root cause?'. This highlights the unreliability of relying solely on cloud-based AI services.

One builder shared findings from testing local LLMs (AI models that run on your own computer, not in the cloud) on their Mac M4 Pro, getting speeds of 3 to 40 tokens/second, showing that running powerful AI locally is becoming feasible on consumer hardware.
Paul Graham, a well-known startup founder, suggests that if he were 17, he'd learn how to build LLMs from scratch, emphasizing the foundational importance of this technology.

Some argue that 'coding is a solved problem' because AI agents can now take a task, write code, test it, and fix it, suggesting that the value shifts to defining tasks and verifying results, rather than just writing code.

cards.opportunity: Everyone's scrambling to build AI agents, but the real pain point is giving them reliable, *personal* context that doesn't disappear when the cloud service goes down. Think about building a supercharged, private 'brain' for *your* computer that captures everything you do (like that 'Screen memory' app, but smarter) and serves it up to any local LLM or agent. The first person to ship a robust, easy-to-use desktop app that acts as a local, always-on context provider for private LLMs will own the 'personal AI assistant' market that actually works, and you could probably prototype the data capture this weekend.
